title: Trump: Stephen Miller tells Justice Dept. to increase child separation
description_short: Trump: Stephen Miller tells Justice Dept. to increase child separation
description_medium: Stephen Miller questioned why some border prosecutors were declining to prosecute migrants who arrived with young children. His email to a Justice Department official cited an article describing that practice. The supplied timeline connects this intervention to a subsequent meeting in which Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein demanded prosecution regardless of children's ages.
description_long:
Stephen Miller questioned why some border prosecutors were declining to prosecute migrants who arrived with young children. His email to a Justice Department official cited an article describing that practice. The supplied timeline connects this intervention to a subsequent meeting in which Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein demanded prosecution regardless of children's ages.

The meeting occurred approximately a week after Miller's May 14, 2018 email. According to notes cited in the linked account, Rosenstein rejected concerns that prosecuting adults would separate children younger than five from their parents. The directive mattered because prosecutors' decisions about charging parents had immediate implications for whether families could remain together.

This entry documents pressure from White House and Justice Department officials on the border prosecution process. It identifies the reported email, the later meeting, and Rosenstein's instruction; it does not establish how many families were separated as a result of this particular exchange or independently resolve individual prosecutors' responses.

title: Trump: Russia infiltrates Antifa groups in Germany to ignite far-right

It cites reporting that sites associated with Antifa West Berlin and Antifa Nord Ost promoted an anti-AfD rally in Berlin while displaying technical connections to infrastructure used by Russian hackers in the 2016 United States election.
description_long:
The linked account describes suspected Russian influence activity involving websites presenting themselves as German anti-fascist groups. It cites reporting that sites associated with Antifa West Berlin and Antifa Nord Ost promoted an anti-AfD rally in Berlin while displaying technical connections to infrastructure used by Russian hackers in the 2016 United States election.

One cited connection was a shared server; another involved an anonymized registration email also used for Russian spearphishing sites. The account situates these findings alongside Russian media support for Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany party. Analysts interpreted the combination as an effort to deepen political division rather than consistently support one ideology.

The evidence described concerns online impersonation, amplification, and technical infrastructure. It does not demonstrate that every anti-fascist group involved was controlled by Russia or that attending a promoted rally indicated Russian affiliation. The parallel with the United States is contextual: influence operations can encourage competing political constituencies while pursuing disruption rather than genuine support for either side.

It accused the intelligence director of unlawfully preventing Congress from receiving information and effectively silencing the whistleblower.

The linked timeline describes the letter as outlining interactions among the intelligence community's inspector general, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the White House, and the Justice Department. Initially anonymous, the whistleblower later identified himself as Max Kennedy Jr. The complaint questioned staffing qualifications and warned that procurement failures could endanger Americans during the pandemic.
description_long:
A volunteer associated with Jared Kushner's coronavirus task force submitted a complaint to Congress alleging serious problems in its effort to procure protective equipment for hospitals. Initially anonymous, the whistleblower later identified himself as Max Kennedy Jr. The complaint questioned staffing qualifications and warned that procurement failures could endanger Americans during the pandemic.

Reporting reproduced in the linked account describes volunteers with little experience in health care, purchasing, or supply-chain management. It also attributes to the complaint an allegation that requests connected to Fox News figures Brian Kilmeade and Jeanine Pirro received attention from the team. Kennedy asked Congress to intervene and later discussed his experience publicly.

The event is the submission of a whistleblower's allegations to the House Oversight Committee, not an adjudication of the task force's conduct. Its significance lies in an insider challenging how an emergency supply operation was staffed and directed. The available material does not quantify deaths caused by the team or establish that every claimed procurement failure resulted from a named official's decision.

title: Trump: Louis DeJoy starts at USPS, mail delays immediately follow

Later reporting described accumulated mail, delayed bills, and veterans waiting for medications, while questions grew about the Postal Service's ability to handle increased election-related mail during the pandemic.
description_long:
Louis DeJoy began work as postmaster general on June 15, 2020. The supplied timeline reports that complaints about unusually slow mail followed within a week. Later reporting described accumulated mail, delayed bills, and veterans waiting for medications, while questions grew about the Postal Service's ability to handle increased election-related mail during the pandemic.

The linked account places the delays alongside rapid operational changes before the November election. It cites Postal Service insiders who said the agency had generally avoided substantial changes close to a general election. Initial attention to the disruption was limited, with pandemic-related pressure offering an alternative explanation before broader reporting emerged.

The chronology establishes that DeJoy's arrival and subsequent complaints occurred close together. It does not by itself identify the cause of every delayed delivery or prove an intention to obstruct voting. The practical concern was whether a heavily relied-upon national delivery service could maintain ordinary operations while preparing for unusually large volumes of mailed ballots.

title: Trump Admin. gives terrorist treatment to International Criminal Court

The action occurred while the court was investigating alleged war crimes in Afghanistan involving Americans. The linked account describes restrictions on United States assets and transactions, with possible sanctions for people assisting relevant investigations.
description_long:
The Trump administration imposed sanctions on International Criminal Court prosecutor Fatou Bensouda and official Phakiso Mochochoko on September 2, 2020. The action occurred while the court was investigating alleged war crimes in Afghanistan involving Americans. The linked account describes restrictions on United States assets and transactions, with possible sanctions for people assisting relevant investigations.

Secretary of State Mike Pompeo presented the court's pursuit of Americans as the reason for the measures. Human Rights Watch's Richard Dicker criticized the sanctions as an obstruction of international justice. The court's role is to prosecute specified international crimes where applicable jurisdiction exists and national authorities are unwilling or unable to prosecute.

The sanctions targeted officials conducting an investigation; they did not establish whether particular Americans were guilty of war crimes. The dispute concerned accountability, jurisdiction, and the use of financial restrictions against court personnel. The supplied account records the administration's action and criticism of its effect on investigations, without demonstrating that sanctions ended the Afghanistan proceedings.

title: Trump: Russian agent Michael Caputo celebrates controlling CDC's COVID reports

The linked account cites an email obtained by a House coronavirus oversight subcommittee.
description_long:
An email dated September 9, 2020 shows HHS adviser Paul Alexander celebrating changes he said the CDC made after his pressure. Alexander wrote to public affairs chief Michael Caputo about revisions to scientific reporting, including language concerning coronavirus transmission among younger people. The linked account cites an email obtained by a House coronavirus oversight subcommittee.

The reporting describes Alexander claiming success over two examples of changes to the CDC's weekly morbidity and mortality reports. Those publications communicate scientific findings to public health professionals and the public. His email presented editorial changes as political victories, raising questions about interference by appointees in material ordinarily treated as scientific reporting.

The documented issue is Alexander's asserted influence and Caputo's receipt of the message. His celebration does not independently establish the full reason CDC staff adopted particular wording, nor quantify resulting health effects. The source's broader characterization of Caputo as a Russian agent is not substantiated by this email, which supports a narrower account of pressure on CDC communications.

description_long:

The claim portrayed Clinton as seeking to create a scandal linking Donald Trump to Russia's hacking of Democratic Party material. Ratcliffe's disclosure went to Senate Judiciary Committee chairman Lindsey Graham and drew objections from Democrats and former intelligence officials.

The linked reporting says the Senate Intelligence Committee had previously encountered and dismissed the allegation during its bipartisan investigation of Russian election interference. Critics argued that releasing unverified information from an adversary risked amplifying disinformation in the United States. Their objection concerned both the claim's reliability and the manner of its public disclosure.

The entry records an official declassification and the controversy it generated. It does not treat a Russian intelligence assessment as proof that Clinton directed a fabricated scandal. title: Trump: Republicans ask the Supreme Court to block Pennsylvania ballots
description_short: Trump: Republicans ask the Supreme Court to block Pennsylvania ballots
description_medium: Pennsylvania Republicans asked the United States Supreme Court on November 6, 2020 to segregate late-arriving absentee ballots and stop processing them. The dispute concerned a state-court extension allowing eligible ballots mailed before polls closed to arrive through Friday. Pennsylvania's secretary of state had already directed officials to keep those ballots separate from other votes.
description_long:
Pennsylvania Republicans asked the United States Supreme Court on November 6, 2020 to segregate late-arriving absentee ballots and stop processing them. The dispute concerned a state-court extension allowing eligible ballots mailed before polls closed to arrive through Friday. Pennsylvania's secretary of state had already directed officials to keep those ballots separate from other votes.

The linked account describes the Supreme Court's evening response as requiring segregation and a separate tally without granting the request to halt counting. This distinction matters: keeping ballots identifiable preserves the possibility of a later legal ruling, whereas suspending processing would delay the counting operation itself. The filing sought to challenge the state court's extension.

The event documents litigation over receipt deadlines after Election Day. It does not establish that late-arriving ballots were fraudulent or that excluding them would change Pennsylvania's result. The source's contemporary discussion of vote margins reflects the count at that time, rather than a final determination of the election's outcome or the merits of every ballot challenge.

title: Trump: 32 Republican ‘Election Fraud' Claims, Debunked by Isaac Saul

description_medium: Journalist Isaac Saul assembled a detailed rebuttal of claims that the 2020 election had been stolen through widespread fraud. The linked timeline reproduces portions of his expanding social media thread, covering allegations involving poll watchers, voter records, vote-reporting jumps, and absentee ballots. It presents explanations for viral material circulated after Donald Trump's electoral defeat.
description_long:
Journalist Isaac Saul assembled a detailed rebuttal of claims that the 2020 election had been stolen through widespread fraud. The linked timeline reproduces portions of his expanding social media thread, covering allegations involving poll watchers, voter records, vote-reporting jumps, and absentee ballots. It presents explanations for viral material circulated after Donald Trump's electoral defeat.

Among the examples discussed were covered windows at a Detroit counting location, a Michigan reporting error, and Wisconsin claims overlooking same-day voter registration. Saul also explained that Milwaukee's centrally counted absentee ballots could produce a large change in reported totals when released together. These examples distinguish unusual-looking images or numbers from evidence of unlawful voting.

The entry records a published fact-checking effort rather than a court finding resolving every election allegation. Its supplied title refers to thirty-two claims, while the reproduced text describes an evolving thread. Individual rebuttals depend on their accompanying local reporting and official explanations; the existence of the thread alone is not a substitute for evidence about any separate claim.

The source does not identify who issued the instruction to stop publication or establish the motive behind it. Nor does withholding a statement prove that the underlying assessment changed. description_long:
Republican lawmakers and sympathetic media figures promoted claims that Antifa was responsible for the January 6 Capitol attack. The linked account describes a Washington Times report asserting that facial recognition had identified an anti-fascist participant. The newspaper retracted that account after the technology company disputed it, but the allegation continued circulating in political and media commentary.

Representative Matt Gaetz cited the story in Congress. The source says one person misidentified in the narrative, Jake Angeli, was a Trump supporter associated with QAnon. It also describes the company's reported identification of a QAnon supporter and people connected with neo-Nazi groups, rather than confirmation of the newspaper's claim.

The event concerns an unsupported explanation being amplified despite correction of a cited evidentiary basis. It does not require claiming that the political affiliation of every person present had already been established. The specific problem was turning disputed identification claims into a broad account of responsibility for the attack, diverting attention from documented participants and the circumstances of the assault.

title: Trump: Pelosi worried about Trump using nukes, calls Defense Dept.

In a letter describing the call, she portrayed the outgoing president as dangerous and urged measures to protect the public during the remaining days of his administration.
description_long:
House Speaker Nancy Pelosi spoke with Joint Chiefs chairman Mark Milley on January 8, 2021 about safeguards against Donald Trump initiating military action or ordering a nuclear strike. In a letter describing the call, she portrayed the outgoing president as dangerous and urged measures to protect the public during the remaining days of his administration.

The linked account explains that military officials could reject unlawful orders or seek legal review, but could not simply remove the president from the lawful chain of command. Trump remained commander in chief unless removed through the applicable constitutional process. The call therefore did not by itself transfer presidential military authority to Pelosi or Milley.

The entry records Pelosi's concern and request for information about precautions, rather than evidence that Trump had ordered a nuclear attack. It also places her subsequent demand for resignation or impeachment alongside the discussion. Any assurance Pelosi took from the conversation should be distinguished from a legally established change in who could issue lawful military orders.
